full_text:
I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing. It’s a 2 year project looking at women in engineering, across all the subjects and we’re mainly looking at people that are going on work placements, at the end of this year.  Are you going on placement or not?

Yes, I am.

OK, We’re interviewing people that aren’t going on placement as well and we’re looking at women’s experiences in education so far and about why they want to do engineering and what they’re hoping to get from their placement and things like that. I’ll start off asking you like a few questions about your background and things like that and why you wanted to do engineering.  Is it chemical engineering you’re doing?

Chemical engineering, yes.

Did you do ‘A’ levels?

Yes I did.

What did you do ‘A’ levels in?

I did ‘A’ levels in Maths, IT and chemistry

OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Originally, I’m from [country], from a high school in the Caribbean and then doing ‘A’ level I went to a school in London, that’s in South – South West London.  It’s somewhere in the region near [place], so the school was made of a girls school and a guys school but (lost words).

Ok, have you got any work experience in the industry at all?

No, I haven’t – this will be my first.

OK, What do your parents do are either of them engineers at all?

Er, no they’re not – they’re retired.

OK. That’s fine.  Did you come to the UK before you started doing ‘A’ levels?

Yes, (lost words)

OK so when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Ah, I’ve always had a notion of like doing engineering. I think I was kind of pushed towards that side because I had a brother who was – a much older brother, who was a (?) engineer and he started off doing chemical – not chemical, electrical engineering but he dropped out, so… (Ok) And because we were really close, I wanted to do some engineering.  But originally it was mechanical. (Ok) I wanted to work on cars but found out it wasn’t all as it seemed.

OK, when did you decide that – did you start doing a mechanical degree?

No, I didn’t – I went to – doing ‘A’ level, my father (lost words).  I liked chemistry, since then I’ve always wanted to do chemical engineering – I chose chemical engineering.  Er, I’ve (lost words) like last year, coming back.  Don’t know then – you (lost words) but in the end I wanted a degree (lost words) engineering.

OK, when you were at school did you have any careers advice or anything like that?
Did anyone particularly – apart from maybe your brother – did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from doing engineering?

Er, there wasn’t much encouragement for doing engineering at the school I went to. There’s more – probably doing biological science or chemistry, microbiology, something of that sort.  But there wasn’t - I think because the character of it - it was a small one. It had to cater for the high school kids. It wasn’t much focussed on the sixth form so I guess we just – it was (?) like for (filling out the UCAS form?) thinking of what options you’d like to do, that’s when you start like speaking to your head at sixth form and trying to see the options that are there, but then we had a (series?) about a different university, but that’s basically it.

OK, did your tutor at ‘A’ levels know that you maybe wanted to do engineering or did you decide later on that you wanted to do engineering?

I knew that I wanted to do er science and back home, I was in science stream because when you had to decide – I think by the time you are 13 you had decide, you’re either in the higher stream or business, because the high school was structured in such a way that after I did – prio to becoming 14, you’ve chosen erm business ot science, or general, which is the Arts thing.  So – and then you do a further 2 year at the high school, finish off doing your chosen field, so I did science and I was thinking I was going to end up doing something with science, biology or chemistry or something.

OK, how did you decide to come to the UK to do it?

Oh my Dad actually lived here for some time, you know.  And my sister came here and my grandparents worked here, but they’re back in [country] now.

OK, could you have done engineering in [country]?

Yeah, it was – at the time it wasn’t – I probably would never have done chemical engineering (yeah) it’s not so (?),  Actually, when I realised that – yes, we do chemical engineering at Uni.  (laughter).  I think – I think they’re more based on my – the electrical engineering, doctor, lawyer, so…

OK, when you were looking at courses at university – did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich placement year?

Yeah, that one appealed to me er mainly because I wanted a feel of what I was gonna go into. After spending so much years at university, I’d like to be in like a permanent job that I really like, so I thought better if I had a year out and then speaking to [name], he is a lecturer, he advised that that is kind of best.

Ok, how did you decide to come and do chemical engineering at [this university] then?

Erm, at [this university]?  I actually went to a foundation year after I did ‘A’ levels, didn’t do well.  And I did a foundation year at [university 2], and at that time my (?) was like in study I do chemical engineering, so what happened I started looking at different – all my usual ones, I’m not sure – I really didn’t know what was happening because everything happened fast.  Because I started coming and I didn’t know anything, like they’re closing down or anything, so it was quite a shock and everything just went woosh.  We had to decide.  We didn’t even know if they were going to place us in another university but later there was a protest and then it was – there was rumour about us moving to [university 3].  Looking at the league - I started – you know – to do my own research of where I could go and that would offer a sandwich course (Yeah) preferably somewhere similar to [university 2], because [university 2] had like a – you could have 6 months – they did 2 separate placements – 6 months each.  And I looked up the league tables on the Internet and looked over quite a lot.  So there was like [university 4], then [university 5] and then I did a – I think the first one who replied was [this university] and they told me to fax my results for the first semester results and everything, and then later up they call me for an interview, so that they can have a chat with me and I can see the place.  And I came down and it’s – and then I liked the place and it was nice quiet town so that appealed to me. (OK) Because being in London for erm ‘A’ level, was not a good experience.  It was crowded I think, and busy.  So it was the nice things and the school – the university, had a lot to offer.  They had a good reputation with companies here so that was…

But it’s not a 6 month placement?

No it’s a one year which I was late – I started erm, I was made to follow that.  A lot of companies like prefer if you have like a longer time being a part of a placement rather than the 6 months.

OK, that’s fine.  When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

I knew that erm I think it became quite obvious – it was male dominated but the chemical engineer aspect tended to go – they used to have a lot of (army?) people girls. I think they have – (I read?) they have bigger - er, females for engineering compared with the rest.

Yeah, how many girls are on your course?

Oh, it’s not bad – is it over 20?

Out of how many?

There’s 40 of us, but the intake for mechanical engineers, it’s quite low.

So it’s quite even really.

Yeah, I think it’s quite even. I think there are a few extra boys, but we’re quite even.

OK, do you think that when you go and work in the industry, it’ll be as even or do you think that will be more male dominated?

I think where I’ll be working it’s mostly – yeah, male dominated, yeah.

Does that bother you at all?

No it doesn’t, ‘cos I’ve been – I have been like for years working with guys.  In high school, I was in science and then I have spent plenty of time with more guys.  In my high school class it was almost 50 students, of which only 10 girls.  So…

Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Yes, I do think so but whether it’s on – they have someone to go and talk to them (yeah) because apart from that they’ll tend to stick to the old thing that I like.  Really males – only males can do engineering it isn’t for girls – that will stick.

Yes, do you think that’s because they don’t know what it really is like – so they need more information really?

Yeah, I don’t think so, because growing up I didn’t think – I thought engineers were like proper mechanics stuff like that and then they fixed – you know – anything you have a problem with they’ll just fix but I mean it’s more – until my brother was going into that field.

OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

I think erm you have to work well, team work is quite important, erm, communication skills, paying attention to detail – that’s quite important because when you’re working on different design it’s kind of important to get things right.  Erm, it’s all (?) workers I should think.

Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female?

I think females tend to pay more attention to detail.  I think guys are – I don’t think – we probably have less chance of coming up with bright ideas and being able to move forward with it – it’s a bit limited.  Guys tend to have this idea and get really excited about it and they push it through while we tend to be a bit dull.  I think – well based on myself and the other girls.

Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Ah, advantages?  There could be.  Guys might help you with tightening bolts or untightening, because they think you’re too weak but I mean it’s…

Has that happened to you?

Yeah, I worked with this guy who once we’re doing this experiment and we had to undo a bolt and stuff like that and he offered to do it.  And I went, no, no, I can do it – I’m taking part – yes, but I mean apart from that I don’t think there’s…

OK. I’m going to ask you a bit about the course now. Has the degree been what you expected it to be?

Well, it has been but even though I did expect it to be kind of challenging, it’s still surprising it’s so hard.  You have to work.  (Yeah) ‘Cos it’s amazing how time flies for me like – well with my first year, like normal design work, because they help you build up communication skills and team work and you have a feeling of what it would be like working in industry with other people.  And then you just need to manage your time so being quite organised is quite important and last time I found myself not being organised.

OK, what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Ah, I like the team work.  I like team work even though these last times they are – like they’re really, really difficult.  You become so aware of all your other peers being so difficult to get along with especially when you have to make a decision and then you have to make a compromise and it’s even hard reaching a compromise stage.  But I mean it’s good fun, you learn more about yourself.  I mean I would never have thought I could do you know, the subject teaching or I could be a leader for our team and I’ve been able to do that and then I’ve also been able to sit on the other side, and know what it is like to be led by someone, you know.

Do you think that doing that sort of work will help you when you are working in the industry?

Yeah, I do think so because I mean it becomes really tough when you have – say you’re ding a design and people don’t pull their own weight.  What do you do about stuff sitting there?  Do you just slack off as well?  But then, OK but how you can motivate other people – some people you can’t, but you can at least try.  It’s something fun I think it will be even (worse?) when I go into industry ‘cos then I’ll be able to apply what I’ve learnt and see if this is really what I want to do.  Cos that was one of the main reasons for me wanting to do the placement.  Is this the course I really want - erm, career path I really want to go on.

OK, when you do group work then, do you get to choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

Er, a few times – ah really, you rarely get to choose who you want to work with. We have a design group now – we’re picked. I don’t know how they do it, but they pick you.  They pick you in such a way that throughout the year you never work with the same person.  That’s the aim.

Do you like that?

Well, I understand what they’re doing and I kind of – when you have deadlines to meet and you’re not working well with this party you’re thinking oh goodness – why, why, why?  But then, you actually appreciate at the end, when you do your presentation – present the design – it might not be like as you want but it, to me, for me then you realise the importance of doing all this exercise.  So that’s what I’ve come to learn.

When you’re working in groups do you prefer to work with men or women or aren’t you really bothered?

I’m not bothered.  Once I think – once we’re able to get the job, do the job and everybody is like really into what they’re doing and does their job properly and you know, you communicate a lot, help each other out, once that’s fine, I’m fine.

Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to doing team work?

I would think each individual brain brings different characteristics. I’m trying to think about sorts of make up on any occasions where there was the trait for just males but I can’t think of any.

No that’s fine. Is there anything bad about your course that you wish you could change or the way in which you work like...?

There’s nothing bad about, it’s just we have like a packed - if you compare to humanities, like history – they have 6 hours – but then they have to do their own personal study to make up.  But we have like packed hours and we also have our personal study.  So I mean like I’d love to take part in – they have community action here, but they have the training to take part like in (?) programme – stuff like that, it kind of conflicts with my lectures so I’ve just let it pass.

Do you think that the fact that you do so many hours will help you when you start work?

Yeah, I think so because then you’re more used to working these long hours or a full day and then, you won’t be like really tired or not able to focus on something for a long period of time.

OK, that’s great.  Have you had any female lecturers?

Er, no I haven’t – none at all.  I’ve had – well, no, I don’t think there is one.  No I haven’t.

Would you find it encouraging if you did have any female lecturers?

I’ve never really thought about it.  Well, I keep – yeah, it could be encouraging but I think it would be – yeah, it could be.

In a sort of – if they can do it?

Yeah, you can do it as well.  That’s back to the notion of always start off (?) you – male.  It’s something that…

Do you think that’s something to do with the subject that you’re doing or just…?

I think it’s the subject.  Yeah, ‘cos I think probably humanities and other courses they tend to – will have females in, but still I don’t think there’s a lot of female lecturers.

OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female and male students the same?

Definitely – and I definitely think so in my course. I’ve never come across or have any type of treatment or otherwise.  I think we’re – basically we’re treated equal.

Ok, that’s good have you got a personal tutor?

Oh yes,

Are they male as well?

Male, yes.

Would you rather have a female personal tutor or doesn’t it bother you?

It doesn’t bother me, I get along with my tutors especially when he’s lecturing me, so I can go and ask that same day.  Often I try (??) to guess things and I give up.  He makes it much clearer.

OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree?

Since I’ve started I’ve met like students who are engineering – women who have been doing like er (?) experience from my country, and it’s quite like encouraging in the fact that I never thought, especially when I met someone who is doing her PhD and doing her degree in chemical engineering and she’s from my country.  I never thought we did that before or anybody back home did it, but it’s quite encouraging and they’ve been like, they’re probably in their thirties and they’ve had jobs back home and they decided to go study so, they let me think that maybe one day I’m gonna do further studies and do a PhD.  Even though at the moment I don’t think I’ll do it – but then speaking to them they said they also had that kind of idea, oh they’ll never get back into education then here they are.  And I’ve also like – it’s been – and new (?) people ‘cos I’m in the woman in engineering society – find me, like a lot of other girls, doing engineering course who – they’re probably, you know, more male dominated engineering course than I am, so I meet and share our views, it’s quite surprising what information you can get.

And has being part of that group, been supportive do you think?

Yeah, it’s quite supportive because not only do we support each other but also what we do is like all go on a programme that we go out.  We mentor girls, encouraging them into engineering – so that’s quite good.

That sounds good. What bits of being at university and the teaching and advice that you might have had, do you think that you’ll take onto placement with you?

I’ll probably – don’t be afraid to ask questions during your placement.  That is like the most – probably the most important side of your degree.  It’s not whole but it helps, as I mean, there’s so much you can get from the placement.  Now when you come back and you – you see things on your course in a different light.  Things you – I think it probably will make you more – either more enthusiastic about your course or not enthusiastic.  But my - the majority of the people – you are more into your course.  You are – you are more open minded.  I think you tend to look at problems in the course design work differently based on the skills that you’ve picked up on your placement, so I mean…

What about the other way round, do you think that you’ll take any skills from the course, to the placement?

Yeah, I would. I definitely think team working here – at this moment I think I can work with any team.  Anyone, irrespective of the individual.  Once, because the aim of team work is, irrespective of your personal feelings, to just get the job done and do it to a good standard.

What about the technical side of things?

Technical – well, I’m hoping – I’m hoping I’ll be able to bring that work doing it on a placement, but I’m not quite sure because mine isn’t so much of a technical – technical.  I’ll be working with computers – so what we’ll be doing is testing software for companies like – well [company] will use for their (??) and stuff like that.  But yeah, I will take some technical knowledge ‘cos that means I’m using a programme called – I’m going to be using a programme called Isis and I’m going to be working for the company who made that – that programme, so..

Oh excellent, who is the company that you’re going to?

[Company].  It’s based in [town].

OK, well it should be good then.

Yeah, well I quite like that.

OK, do you feel like you’re ready to go on placement now or would you have rather gone earlier or later?

I think – I’m not sure if it’s because of  the mindset that after second year, I’ll go on placement – but yeah, I’m ready.  And I’m really ready I think it will do me a lot of good maybe because you can take a break on all those jobs and I – it will actually probably get me more motivated.

Yeah. Do you think that the university could do anything else to help prepare you for what to expect on your placement?

Well, my department has been doing a lot – I’m not aware about the other departments that they’re (?).  Yeah, I think that we have session on like getting your CV ready, how to do interviews and also what – like the team building experience, also contributes to (??).  So what to expect, during your placement year, so I think they’ve done a lot and you are actually – there is no case scenario where you could actually try for work or try to go in there because you might end up going to a company that somebody shared their experience with.  And you prepare for that and then yours might be just (different?) so I mean…I think if you have the main skills of team work and you are focussed and aim to get the job done to a high standard, then your experience should be special.

And have the department or the university, have they taken a role in helping you find the actual placement?  Is that …

Yeah, my department they’re active.  I mean each – I think it was September, ending of September we had our first company on our notice and then we had like loads so it’s quite – they’re quite helpful, the chemical engineering department, here.

Did companies come in and talk to you as well, or…?

We have erm the careers service here provide that kind of system, with getting the companies here and then you can attend them now.  They will do a presentation.  So we – I think that’s also arranged with the different departments around.  So when we’re doing – it depends – during our interview stage some companies might decide to have like come a day before, they do a presentation so you get to know more about them.  So I choose on the day.  So that’s like prior to doing your interview, doing their presentations.  Yeah, it’s adequate.

OK, what attracted you to the company that you’re going to then?

Oh, well I – I have no clue what it was like.  It was quite amazing when they phoned me up and I was like OK.  I’m doing exam right now so I’ll just – if they could call me back another time and they said OK, that’s fine.  And then I just went to the – to the receptionist and asked, who was it, who are they, and she was like OK, this is what I have on them and then I looked on their web site and did my research and I was like – I still was – it still wasn’t clear what they were all about. I knew they were software programmers – well a processing engineer – it was until that day I went for the er, the interview and then they started telling me a bit more about themselves and what we’ll be doing as a placement student.  Yeah, and I really wanted to get the job.

Did you apply to any other companies?

Yeah, I applied to like other companies.  Yeah, [company] – I applied to [company], I can’t – didn’t get an invite to interview but got shortlisted.

When you’ve been looking at companies have you been looking at anything like the salary you’re going to get or the training opportunities or like career prospects, anything like that?

Yeah, I do look at all – oh the salary’s a big one (laughs) ‘cos I like to look at the salary.  But after you look at the salary then you can calm down and then you start looking – oh, training aspect as well is quite important.  Rather important – if later, having done your placement and you re-experience it, come back and work for them.  But that was also, so I also took that into account and also just the size – the size of the company and er future growth – whether or not they are like a sub-company, depends – they might need – so it decentralises, sort of they are cut in half – so you probably wouldn’t want to like be tied to a company.  It’s a good experience but a lot of people when – when you tend to have your placement, you want to probably be able to go back there and there’s a possibility that you go back there and work for them, so I looked – I was also looking at the fact that I’m – having been chosen to work for your company, would I get a bit of preference – being a graduate.  And a lot of companies, they do that so that opens…

With this company, do you think that you’ll have that opportunity to go back?

I – it depends if they’re (?) because they’re quite a small company, so it just depends like. I think I’ll probably have the opportunity if …

Did the company tell you much about the actual type of work you would be doing then?

Yes, they did. I’ll be working testing software that would basically – a programme used by a lot of the (processing?) companies – pharmaceuticals, (lost words).  It’s assessing their needs for them, for the company and what we’ll do before it goes.  Er, we test it to make sure it meets er the buyers requirements and constantly test it.  And we also erm design software that would – on like all the jobs (lost words?) for particular of companies. (Lost words)

OK, did you ever have the opportunity to get a sponsorship and be a sponsored student, or not?

Er, sponsored – sponsored as in?

I think some companies will sponsor a student while they’re at university, and they’ll get money and then they can get work in the summer and on the placements but then they have to go back and work for them when they’ve finished, but I don’t know whether it’s open to everybody or it’s just certain departments but…

I think, I haven’t been sponsored but I mean, there might be one person in my department who has been sponsored.  And I think there are, with a lot of companies, you have to have worked for them in your gap year prior to coming to university.  But there are some courses that they are – they have a lot of sponsored students.

Do you think that’s a good idea, on that?

I think it’s kind of a good idea, especially if they give you the leeway of going to work round another company and its business. So I – it is well it’ll obviously be (forgotten?) that yes you have a job at the end of your degree, because I mean all of the graduates, they find it difficult getting – you know it’s (?) scientifical, getting a job.  So I mean that should set you up at least.

OK, what do you think will be the worst things and the best things about going onto a placement?

Er, the worst thing would be not knowing – not knowing what to do.  Which I’m worried. I like to get things done like orderly and perfect, you know?  I don’t like people saying oh, you missed that.  I know it – it’s kind of helpful if they do, but I – I tend to like (?) for perfect and I hope – the worst thing for me would not be able to like – to have my boss view me as like incapable, you know?  Oh, that’s my worst fear.

OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Well, first – well if I’m sick I can’t just not show up.  Or if I have (??) you know, I can’t just not show up, up show up later in the day, which you tend to do – (miss early morning lectures?) and then show up and get the notes.  I mean you are being paid – paid for your job I mean you have a responsibility to the company and I think also to erm your team members who you are working with because if you miss a day while – which could have been avoided, then I mean they would probably have to give me more work to cover up what you were supposed to do.  So I think you have a (?) – the access.  Er, quite – and the fact that and then knowing that you definitely have to get up early in the morning, be on time, 9 till 5 job, you can…

In terms of your career then, what do you think you’ll be doing in 5 years time?

5 years time?  Well right now I’m thinking about joining in the navy.  (Ok)  And so, hopefully, unless the placement changes my mind I’ll probably – if not the navy then definitely into some related aspect of chemical engineering, whether it’s a pharmaceutical company, an oil company or a food company.

And would it be engineering that you’d like to do in the navy?

Yeah, engineering.  I think I’d be mostly based with mechanical engineering.

OK, and what about in say 10 years time?

Well I’ve – whatever job I’m in I’d like to be in a senior role (yes) and I would – well responsibility and also to probably do second (?) where we come up to university/high school and part of you talks.  I mean to encourage more girls and other – into higher education and having the like, (quiet?) picture of what to expect.  ‘Cos I mean, a lot of time, if I had it in high school, someone telling me about chemical engineering, that would’ve been great.  I’d probably know definitely, oh yeah, I’ll definitely go into that.  But we had nothing like that so no subject was (?) because in my country…

So going into the navy then, is that like your ideal career?

Yeah, it would be. I – yeah, officer in the navy.

Yeah, do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to do that?

I sometimes can…

Are there any barriers between you and getting into the navy, or do you think that you will be able to do that?

I should be able to because I’ve spoken to a Lieutenant who comes to the career service.  He explained I just need to like go through, get a good degree, go through physical training er preparation and then there is the Admiral Board, will be doing just team work.  And then pychometric tests. I  mean I actually – I have some experience of doing some (wireless?) for interviews and I – so I think so.

Could you have gone for a placement with the navy?

No they don’t do them.

OK, do you think that you’ll carry on working in the UK, or do you want to travel or do you want to go back to [home country]?

Well, initially I’d like to work here and then I’d like to travel as well, so I wouldn’t mind a company like international, where you could be based

Is that one of the things that attracts you to the navy as well?

Yes, and also the physical aspects about it.  And they have quite good sports programmes.  I mean it’s quite sensible when you think about – and the work they do.  It’s not about just war. I can’t really recall if they actually took part in the war – they just supplied the shipments for the soldiers, ‘cos they are involved in like (?) the defence of like, peace, protection, protecting the coast.  You know there’s a lot of stuff that isn’t about war, just for work as well as the other er forces.  That’s quite well, because of the – (lost words).

Yes, that sounds good.  Do you think that the career prospects, in chemical engineering, are good?

I do think so, that they are good.

Getting into the industry in the first place - do you think that should be OK?  Maybe once you’re in the industry to develop your career?

Yeah, most of the companies I’ve looked at, it’s – I think they are – there would be no problem, if you do your work – I think they expect your working performance – then promotion and development throughout the year will come naturally.  So I don’t think that’s a problem.  And then, for chemical engineering we have a low intake.  It’s UK wide – there’s not a lot of students going in, so, then again there’s not a lot of students go into any engineering course so, but they’re all drying up.  So there shouldn’t be any problem getting a job.  It’s no (women?) for getting the top job – that becomes a problem but I mean – it’s relatively even ground I think.

OK, that’s fine.  Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?  Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Yeah, I’m quite – I’m quite pleased where I’m at, at this point.  And I think there are other things I would have achieved that, ‘cos I still have the options, if I still want to go in the navy, there’s still that option and then there’s other option of going into different aspects of chemical engineer.  And, I think in the end again, engineers are being – we can go into business.  I mean not a lot of business students I know could say they could go into science, but I mean.  There is like an open playing field.

OK, that’s great, what 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

Oh dear.  Well, team work, er being flexible and becoming skilled and I think definitely being able to get the job done.  And to a high standard.

Do you think that the culture is masculine?

I do think so but it’s – I mean if you check from like years ago, through history, it’s kind of females are now coming into engineering.  And it will take a while.  If erm – if I think it’s gonna – we’re gonna have an even – you know, a female ratio, I can’t see but if you can imagine how long it took to get one female or so into engineer then there’s a possibility of having a ratio being half/half.  It will take quite long time.  First you have to change people’s minds – back at high school, and I think that’s all you need.

That’s fine, do you think the fact that it is so masculine will cause you any problems at all?

Er, I think it will cause me probably problems.  No, I think well especially not in my field – chemical engineer because I mean, lots of males – they have to work with females and I mentioned before about the ratio.

OK, that’s great – that’s just about it really. One thing I will ask you is, is engineering so male dominated in [home country]?

It’s definitely male (back?), it’s really male dominated. I think even worse than here because I mean when think of engineering – you’d rather, they’d rather ah, you’d appear to them as teachers.  You’d rather be important through teaching or influential through teaching, doctoring you know lawyer – and then there’s a business aspect and engineer.  But I mean just as it is developing here, it’s slowly – it’s slowly getting there but it’s really – I think on a whole, world wide, it’s male dominated near enough and I think because of what we’ve learnt growing up and also community that you’ve lived and stuff.

OK, thanks very much.

turns.text: I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing. It’s a 2 year project looking at women in engineering, across all the subjects and we’re mainly looking at people that are going on work placements, at the end of this year. Are you going on placement or not? Yes, I am. OK, We’re interviewing people that aren’t going on placement as well and we’re looking at women’s experiences in education so far and about why they want to do engineering and what they’re hoping to get from their placement and things like that. I’ll start off asking you like a few questions about your background and things like that and why you wanted to do engineering. Is it chemical engineering you’re doing? Chemical engineering, yes. Did you do ‘A’ levels? Yes I did. What did you do ‘A’ levels in? I did ‘A’ levels in Maths, IT and chemistry OK, and what type of school did you go to? Originally, I’m from [country], from a high school in the Caribbean and then doing ‘A’ level I went to a school in London, that’s in South – South West London. It’s somewhere in the region near [place], so the school was made of a girls school and a guys school but (lost words). Ok, have you got any work experience in the industry at all? No, I haven’t – this will be my first. OK, What do your parents do are either of them engineers at all? Er, no they’re not – they’re retired. OK. That’s fine. Did you come to the UK before you started doing ‘A’ levels? Yes, (lost words) OK so when and why do you think that you decided to do engineering? Ah, I’ve always had a notion of like doing engineering. I think I was kind of pushed towards that side because I had a brother who was – a much older brother, who was a (?) engineer and he started off doing chemical – not chemical, electrical engineering but he dropped out, so… (Ok) And because we were really close, I wanted to do some engineering. But originally it was mechanical. (Ok) I wanted to work on cars but found out it wasn’t all as it seemed. OK, when did you decide that – did you start doing a mechanical degree? No, I didn’t – I went to – doing ‘A’ level, my father (lost words). I liked chemistry, since then I’ve always wanted to do chemical engineering – I chose chemical engineering. Er, I’ve (lost words) like last year, coming back. Don’t know then – you (lost words) but in the end I wanted a degree (lost words) engineering. OK, when you were at school did you have any careers advice or anything like that? Did anyone particularly – apart from maybe your brother – did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from doing engineering? Er, there wasn’t much encouragement for doing engineering at the school I went to. There’s more – probably doing biological science or chemistry, microbiology, something of that sort. But there wasn’t - I think because the character of it - it was a small one. It had to cater for the high school kids. It wasn’t much focussed on the sixth form so I guess we just – it was (?) like for (filling out the UCAS form?) thinking of what options you’d like to do, that’s when you start like speaking to your head at sixth form and trying to see the options that are there, but then we had a (series?) about a different university, but that’s basically it. OK, did your tutor at ‘A’ levels know that you maybe wanted to do engineering or did you decide later on that you wanted to do engineering? I knew that I wanted to do er science and back home, I was in science stream because when you had to decide – I think by the time you are 13 you had decide, you’re either in the higher stream or business, because the high school was structured in such a way that after I did – prio to becoming 14, you’ve chosen erm business ot science, or general, which is the Arts thing. So – and then you do a further 2 year at the high school, finish off doing your chosen field, so I did science and I was thinking I was going to end up doing something with science, biology or chemistry or something. OK, how did you decide to come to the UK to do it? Oh my Dad actually lived here for some time, you know. And my sister came here and my grandparents worked here, but they’re back in [country] now. OK, could you have done engineering in [country]? Yeah, it was – at the time it wasn’t – I probably would never have done chemical engineering (yeah) it’s not so (?), Actually, when I realised that – yes, we do chemical engineering at Uni. (laughter). I think – I think they’re more based on my – the electrical engineering, doctor, lawyer, so… OK, when you were looking at courses at university – did you always know that you wanted to do a sandwich placement year? Yeah, that one appealed to me er mainly because I wanted a feel of what I was gonna go into. After spending so much years at university, I’d like to be in like a permanent job that I really like, so I thought better if I had a year out and then speaking to [name], he is a lecturer, he advised that that is kind of best. Ok, how did you decide to come and do chemical engineering at [this university] then? Erm, at [this university]? I actually went to a foundation year after I did ‘A’ levels, didn’t do well. And I did a foundation year at [university 2], and at that time my (?) was like in study I do chemical engineering, so what happened I started looking at different – all my usual ones, I’m not sure – I really didn’t know what was happening because everything happened fast. Because I started coming and I didn’t know anything, like they’re closing down or anything, so it was quite a shock and everything just went woosh. We had to decide. We didn’t even know if they were going to place us in another university but later there was a protest and then it was – there was rumour about us moving to [university 3]. Looking at the league - I started – you know – to do my own research of where I could go and that would offer a sandwich course (Yeah) preferably somewhere similar to [university 2], because [university 2] had like a – you could have 6 months – they did 2 separate placements – 6 months each. And I looked up the league tables on the Internet and looked over quite a lot. So there was like [university 4], then [university 5] and then I did a – I think the first one who replied was [this university] and they told me to fax my results for the first semester results and everything, and then later up they call me for an interview, so that they can have a chat with me and I can see the place. And I came down and it’s – and then I liked the place and it was nice quiet town so that appealed to me. (OK) Because being in London for erm ‘A’ level, was not a good experience. It was crowded I think, and busy. So it was the nice things and the school – the university, had a lot to offer. They had a good reputation with companies here so that was… But it’s not a 6 month placement? No it’s a one year which I was late – I started erm, I was made to follow that. A lot of companies like prefer if you have like a longer time being a part of a placement rather than the 6 months. OK, that’s fine. When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated? I knew that erm I think it became quite obvious – it was male dominated but the chemical engineer aspect tended to go – they used to have a lot of (army?) people girls. I think they have – (I read?) they have bigger - er, females for engineering compared with the rest. Yeah, how many girls are on your course? Oh, it’s not bad – is it over 20? Out of how many? There’s 40 of us, but the intake for mechanical engineers, it’s quite low. So it’s quite even really. Yeah, I think it’s quite even. I think there are a few extra boys, but we’re quite even. OK, do you think that when you go and work in the industry, it’ll be as even or do you think that will be more male dominated? I think where I’ll be working it’s mostly – yeah, male dominated, yeah. Does that bother you at all? No it doesn’t, ‘cos I’ve been – I have been like for years working with guys. In high school, I was in science and then I have spent plenty of time with more guys. In my high school class it was almost 50 students, of which only 10 girls. So… Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering? Yes, I do think so but whether it’s on – they have someone to go and talk to them (yeah) because apart from that they’ll tend to stick to the old thing that I like. Really males – only males can do engineering it isn’t for girls – that will stick. Yes, do you think that’s because they don’t know what it really is like – so they need more information really? Yeah, I don’t think so, because growing up I didn’t think – I thought engineers were like proper mechanics stuff like that and then they fixed – you know – anything you have a problem with they’ll just fix but I mean it’s more – until my brother was going into that field. OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer? I think erm you have to work well, team work is quite important, erm, communication skills, paying attention to detail – that’s quite important because when you’re working on different design it’s kind of important to get things right. Erm, it’s all (?) workers I should think. Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female? I think females tend to pay more attention to detail. I think guys are – I don’t think – we probably have less chance of coming up with bright ideas and being able to move forward with it – it’s a bit limited. Guys tend to have this idea and get really excited about it and they push it through while we tend to be a bit dull. I think – well based on myself and the other girls. Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer? Ah, advantages? There could be. Guys might help you with tightening bolts or untightening, because they think you’re too weak but I mean it’s… Has that happened to you? Yeah, I worked with this guy who once we’re doing this experiment and we had to undo a bolt and stuff like that and he offered to do it. And I went, no, no, I can do it – I’m taking part – yes, but I mean apart from that I don’t think there’s… OK. I’m going to ask you a bit about the course now. Has the degree been what you expected it to be? Well, it has been but even though I did expect it to be kind of challenging, it’s still surprising it’s so hard. You have to work. (Yeah) ‘Cos it’s amazing how time flies for me like – well with my first year, like normal design work, because they help you build up communication skills and team work and you have a feeling of what it would be like working in industry with other people. And then you just need to manage your time so being quite organised is quite important and last time I found myself not being organised. OK, what would you say have been the best and the worst things about the course so far? Ah, I like the team work. I like team work even though these last times they are – like they’re really, really difficult. You become so aware of all your other peers being so difficult to get along with especially when you have to make a decision and then you have to make a compromise and it’s even hard reaching a compromise stage. But I mean it’s good fun, you learn more about yourself. I mean I would never have thought I could do you know, the subject teaching or I could be a leader for our team and I’ve been able to do that and then I’ve also been able to sit on the other side, and know what it is like to be led by someone, you know. Do you think that doing that sort of work will help you when you are working in the industry? Yeah, I do think so because I mean it becomes really tough when you have – say you’re ding a design and people don’t pull their own weight. What do you do about stuff sitting there? Do you just slack off as well? But then, OK but how you can motivate other people – some people you can’t, but you can at least try. It’s something fun I think it will be even (worse?) when I go into industry ‘cos then I’ll be able to apply what I’ve learnt and see if this is really what I want to do. Cos that was one of the main reasons for me wanting to do the placement. Is this the course I really want - erm, career path I really want to go on. OK, when you do group work then, do you get to choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups? Er, a few times – ah really, you rarely get to choose who you want to work with. We have a design group now – we’re picked. I don’t know how they do it, but they pick you. They pick you in such a way that throughout the year you never work with the same person. That’s the aim. Do you like that? Well, I understand what they’re doing and I kind of – when you have deadlines to meet and you’re not working well with this party you’re thinking oh goodness – why, why, why? But then, you actually appreciate at the end, when you do your presentation – present the design – it might not be like as you want but it, to me, for me then you realise the importance of doing all this exercise. So that’s what I’ve come to learn. When you’re working in groups do you prefer to work with men or women or aren’t you really bothered? I’m not bothered. Once I think – once we’re able to get the job, do the job and everybody is like really into what they’re doing and does their job properly and you know, you communicate a lot, help each other out, once that’s fine, I’m fine. Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to doing team work? I would think each individual brain brings different characteristics. I’m trying to think about sorts of make up on any occasions where there was the trait for just males but I can’t think of any. No that’s fine. Is there anything bad about your course that you wish you could change or the way in which you work like...? There’s nothing bad about, it’s just we have like a packed - if you compare to humanities, like history – they have 6 hours – but then they have to do their own personal study to make up. But we have like packed hours and we also have our personal study. So I mean like I’d love to take part in – they have community action here, but they have the training to take part like in (?) programme – stuff like that, it kind of conflicts with my lectures so I’ve just let it pass. Do you think that the fact that you do so many hours will help you when you start work? Yeah, I think so because then you’re more used to working these long hours or a full day and then, you won’t be like really tired or not able to focus on something for a long period of time. OK, that’s great. Have you had any female lecturers? Er, no I haven’t – none at all. I’ve had – well, no, I don’t think there is one. No I haven’t. Would you find it encouraging if you did have any female lecturers? I’ve never really thought about it. Well, I keep – yeah, it could be encouraging but I think it would be – yeah, it could be. In a sort of – if they can do it? Yeah, you can do it as well. That’s back to the notion of always start off (?) you – male. It’s something that… Do you think that’s something to do with the subject that you’re doing or just…? I think it’s the subject. Yeah, ‘cos I think probably humanities and other courses they tend to – will have females in, but still I don’t think there’s a lot of female lecturers. OK, do you think that the male lecturers treat the female and male students the same? Definitely – and I definitely think so in my course. I’ve never come across or have any type of treatment or otherwise. I think we’re – basically we’re treated equal. Ok, that’s good have you got a personal tutor? Oh yes, Are they male as well? Male, yes. Would you rather have a female personal tutor or doesn’t it bother you? It doesn’t bother me, I get along with my tutors especially when he’s lecturing me, so I can go and ask that same day. Often I try (??) to guess things and I give up. He makes it much clearer. OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the degree? Since I’ve started I’ve met like students who are engineering – women who have been doing like er (?) experience from my country, and it’s quite like encouraging in the fact that I never thought, especially when I met someone who is doing her PhD and doing her degree in chemical engineering and she’s from my country. I never thought we did that before or anybody back home did it, but it’s quite encouraging and they’ve been like, they’re probably in their thirties and they’ve had jobs back home and they decided to go study so, they let me think that maybe one day I’m gonna do further studies and do a PhD. Even though at the moment I don’t think I’ll do it – but then speaking to them they said they also had that kind of idea, oh they’ll never get back into education then here they are. And I’ve also like – it’s been – and new (?) people ‘cos I’m in the woman in engineering society – find me, like a lot of other girls, doing engineering course who – they’re probably, you know, more male dominated engineering course than I am, so I meet and share our views, it’s quite surprising what information you can get. And has being part of that group, been supportive do you think? Yeah, it’s quite supportive because not only do we support each other but also what we do is like all go on a programme that we go out. We mentor girls, encouraging them into engineering – so that’s quite good. That sounds good. What bits of being at university and the teaching and advice that you might have had, do you think that you’ll take onto placement with you? I’ll probably – don’t be afraid to ask questions during your placement. That is like the most – probably the most important side of your degree. It’s not whole but it helps, as I mean, there’s so much you can get from the placement. Now when you come back and you – you see things on your course in a different light. Things you – I think it probably will make you more – either more enthusiastic about your course or not enthusiastic. But my - the majority of the people – you are more into your course. You are – you are more open minded. I think you tend to look at problems in the course design work differently based on the skills that you’ve picked up on your placement, so I mean… What about the other way round, do you think that you’ll take any skills from the course, to the placement? Oh excellent, who is the company that you’re going to? [Company]. It’s based in [town]. OK, well it should be good then. Yeah, well I quite like that. Do you think that the university could do anything else to help prepare you for what to expect on your placement? Well, my department has been doing a lot – I’m not aware about the other departments that they’re (?). Yeah, I think that we have session on like getting your CV ready, how to do interviews and also what – like the team building experience, also contributes to (??). And have the department or the university, have they taken a role in helping you find the actual placement? Is that … Yeah, my department they’re active. Did companies come in and talk to you as well, or…? We have erm the careers service here provide that kind of system, with getting the companies here and then you can attend them now. So when we’re doing – it depends – during our interview stage some companies might decide to have like come a day before, they do a presentation so you get to know more about them. Yeah, and I really wanted to get the job. Did you apply to any other companies? Yeah, I applied to like other companies. Yeah, [company] – I applied to [company], I can’t – didn’t get an invite to interview but got shortlisted. When you’ve been looking at companies have you been looking at anything like the salary you’re going to get or the training opportunities or like career prospects, anything like that? Yeah, I do look at all – oh the salary’s a big one (laughs) ‘cos I like to look at the salary. But after you look at the salary then you can calm down and then you start looking – oh, training aspect as well is quite important. Rather important – if later, having done your placement and you re-experience it, come back and work for them. I – it depends if they’re (?) because they’re quite a small company, so it just depends like. I think I’ll probably have the opportunity if … Did the company tell you much about the actual type of work you would be doing then? Yes, they did. I’ll be working testing software that would basically – a programme used by a lot of the (processing?) companies – pharmaceuticals, (lost words). It’s assessing their needs for them, for the company and what we’ll do before it goes. Er, we test it to make sure it meets er the buyers requirements and constantly test it. And we also erm design software that would – on like all the jobs (lost words?) for particular of companies. And I think there are, with a lot of companies, you have to have worked for them in your gap year prior to coming to university. But there are some courses that they are – they have a lot of sponsored students. Do you think that’s a good idea, on that? I think it’s kind of a good idea, especially if they give you the leeway of going to work round another company and its business. So I – it is well it’ll obviously be (forgotten?) that yes you have a job at the end of your degree, because I mean all of the graduates, they find it difficult getting – you know it’s (?) scientifical, getting a job. So I mean that should set you up at least. OK, what do you think will be the worst things and the best things about going onto a placement? I know it – it’s kind of helpful if they do, but I – I tend to like (?) for perfect and I hope – the worst thing for me would not be able to like – to have my boss view me as like incapable, you know? Oh, that’s my worst fear. OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university? Well, first – well if I’m sick I can’t just not show up. So I think you have a (?) – the access. Er, quite – and the fact that and then knowing that you definitely have to get up early in the morning, be on time, 9 till 5 job, you can… In terms of your career then, what do you think you’ll be doing in 5 years time? 5 years time? Well right now I’m thinking about joining in the navy. And would it be engineering that you’d like to do in the navy? Yeah, engineering. I think I’d be mostly based with mechanical engineering. OK, and what about in say 10 years time? Well I’ve – whatever job I’m in I’d like to be in a senior role (yes) and I would – well responsibility and also to probably do second (?) where we come up to university/high school and part of you talks. I mean to encourage more girls and other – into higher education and having the like, (quiet?) picture of what to expect. ‘Cos I mean, a lot of time, if I had it in high school, someone telling me about chemical engineering, that would’ve been great. I’d probably know definitely, oh yeah, I’ll definitely go into that. But we had nothing like that so no subject was (?) because in my country… So going into the navy then, is that like your ideal career? Yeah, it would be. I – yeah, officer in the navy. Yeah, do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to do that? I sometimes can… Are there any barriers between you and getting into the navy, or do you think that you will be able to do that? I should be able to because I’ve spoken to a Lieutenant who comes to the career service. He explained I just need to like go through, get a good degree, go through physical training er preparation and then there is the Admiral Board, will be doing just team work. And then pychometric tests. I mean I actually – I have some experience of doing some (wireless?) for interviews and I – so I think so. Could you have gone for a placement with the navy? No they don’t do them. OK, do you think that you’ll carry on working in the UK, or do you want to travel or do you want to go back to [home country]? Well, initially I’d like to work here and then I’d like to travel as well, so I wouldn’t mind a company like international, where you could be based Is that one of the things that attracts you to the navy as well? Yes, and also the physical aspects about it. And they have quite good sports programmes. I mean it’s quite sensible when you think about – and the work they do. It’s not about just war. I can’t really recall if they actually took part in the war – they just supplied the shipments for the soldiers, ‘cos they are involved in like (?) the defence of like, peace, protection, protecting the coast. You know there’s a lot of stuff that isn’t about war, just for work as well as the other er forces. That’s quite well, because of the – (lost words). Yes, that sounds good. Do you think that the career prospects, in chemical engineering, are good? I do think so, that they are good. Getting into the industry in the first place - do you think that should be OK?
